title: Trust in protection
hookLine: he writes that no one can harm the one the Lord protects (Zafarnama)

cards: Who gets to say the word safe? A child in a warm house says it easily. A man who, tradition says, has lost his home and his four sons has every reason never to say it again.
And yet in the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh writes confident lines about exactly that: being protected. He writes them to the emperor himself, whose armies had chased him.
Not a promise of safety from someone who has never been hurt, but from someone who has.

teach.b: Paraphrased, the thought runs like this: what can an enemy do, when the Friend is kind? The One who protects is the Lord, and no one can harm the one the Lord protects. In the letter, the Friend is God.
It can't mean nothing bad will ever happen. The man writing it has already lived through the worst. So protected must mean something else.
Some readers hear it this way: what the emperor can reach is the body, the fort, the family's lives. What he cannot reach is the bond between the Guru and God, and the faith that made the Khalsa.
That's what is held, and that's what no army can take. The trust doesn't make him passive, either. The same letter argues, accuses, and keeps going.
Trust in protection, in the Guru's life, sits right alongside action. It's the floor he stands on while he works, not a reason to stop working. And there's a turn in who he's speaking to.
Telling the emperor, in effect, you cannot harm me is not a boast about armies.
It's a statement about where real power lies.
For the Guru, it lies with the Friend. Sikh prayer, too, asks Waheguru for protection. Read beside this letter, that prayer isn't asking for a life without loss.
It's asking to be held through it.

how: Sikhs recite prayers for protection in the evening, and the Zafarnama's lines on the Lord as protector are recalled in katha as a picture of trust that stands alongside action.

o: a promise that nothing bad will ever happen
a guard of soldiers kept around a leader
faith that God holds you, even through loss

games.q: the letter and its trust: tap the pairs.
p: the body, the fort, the family's lives
the bond between the Guru and God

s: here, protected means nothing bad will ever happen
the man writing it had already lost his home and his sons. protected means held, not untouched.
the letter's trust goes along with argument and action
the same letter accuses, argues and keeps going.
in the letter, the Friend who is kind is a powerful ally at court

games.q: you've lost almost everything, and you're writing to the emperor whose armies did it. what do you say about your safety?
o: say no enemy can harm the one the Lord protects.
threaten him with your remaining army.
games.why: the Guru writes that when the Friend is kind, the enemy can do nothing. a statement about where power lies, not about armies.

practice: Let your weight sink into whatever is holding you up, the chair, the floor, the bed, and notice you didn't have to earn its support.
Bring to mind one worry, don't solve it, set it down beside you where you can still see it, and let yourself be held. If you pray, breathe the name Waheguru; if not, rest in the breath itself.

wordCard.voice: Trust in protection. In the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh writes that no enemy can harm the one the Lord protects, after he had already lost almost everything. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: protected. Trust is the floor to stand on while you work. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Zafarnama (Dasam Granth), the verses on the kind Friend and the Lord as protector
